armed.text: A scarecrow stands in the middle of the room, its post set in a bucket of concrete. Its head is a feed sack drawn tight over something round and heavy, a smile painted on, and its broom-handle arms are held wide on hinged shoulders. It is wearing a coat — a genuinely good waxed coat, corduroy collar, oiled and buttoned to the chin. Behind the post a green sapling has been bent nearly double and tied off with a slipknot, and from the knot a cord runs to the top button.

choices.label: Leave it the coat and back out the way you came
Wedge the slipknot and unbutton it from behind

escaped.text: You leave the coat on the scarecrow, which is the hardest thing you have done since you last left a coat anywhere, and back out with its arms held wide behind you, still offering. The painted smile does not change. It will be standing there dry and warm and buttoned up long after you are neither.

cache_1.text: You jam a stick through the slipknot, unbutton the coat from behind like a valet, and ease it off the scarecrow's shoulders. It is magnificent. Waxed cotton, tartan lining, and a label in the collar that reads {{label}}. It is dry. You had forgotten what dry felt like. The pockets give up a lighter and a fistful of good washers, and the scarecrow stands there in its sacking looking, somehow, cold.

choices.label: Slit the sack and find out what keeps it so plump

cache_2.text: It is not stuffed with straw. Under a top layer for show, the scarecrow is packed shoulder to hip with food: strings of dried apple rings, foil ration bricks, a bag of oats sewn into each leg. The crows never came back. Nobody told the scarecrow, and whoever kept feeding it never told anyone at all. It is the best-fed thing you have met in a month. You leave it the hat.

the_wave.text: You back into one of its outstretched hands and the arm comes round on its hinge like a door in a gale. The glove on the end is stuffed with wet sawdust and about four hundred earwigs, and it bursts across the side of your head, and the earwigs go everywhere earwigs go, which is mostly your collar and at least one ear. You find the last of them hours later, in your rations.

the_hug.text: The knot slips while you are on the second button. The sapling straightens, the arms come round, and the scarecrow takes you in a hug of enormous sincerity, face to face with the feed sack, something in your ribs going click. It smells of damp straw and whatever crawled into the lining to die. The only way out is to wriggle out of your own jacket, canteen and all. The scarecrow is now wearing two coats.

the_stuffing.text: The stuffing is occupied. A family of mice who have been living in the warmest, best-fed body in the building pours out of the slit and up your sleeve, and in the scramble you shoulder the post, and the head — the round, heavy thing in the feed sack is a paint tin — comes down across the bridge of your nose. You sit down hard. The mice take the opportunity to go through your pack.
